title: Columbia and London: The Scholar Who Out-Read His Masters
summary: Subsisting on a single dry crust of bread and tea, Ambedkar studied 18 hours a day, becoming the first person to enter the library at dawn and the last to leave at midnight.
keywords: Columbia and London: The Scholar Who Out-Read His Masters
full_text:
In 1913, funded by a modest scholarship from the enlightened Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad of Baroda, a young man from the Mahar community arrived in New York City: Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar.

Treated as untouchable in his homeland, where he had been forced to sit on gunny sacks outside the school classroom, Columbia University opened a breathtaking world of intellectual freedom.

Ambedkar threw himself into scholarship with superhuman intensity.

While other students enjoyed Broadway theaters and weekend sports, Ambedkar studied eighteen hours every day. He subsisted on a solitary dry roll of bread and coffee to save money for purchasing second-hand books.

The head librarian at Columbia noticed an extraordinary pattern:
At 8:00 AM, the first person waiting outside the locked library doors was the slender Indian scholar.
At 11:00 PM, when the bell rang to clear the desks, the final reader coaxed away from mountainous stacks of books was always Ambedkar!

One evening, the librarian asked:
"Mr. Ambedkar, you are burning your eyes out. Other students study to secure comfortable careers. Why do you torment yourself with eighteen hours of ceaseless reading?"

Ambedkar wiped his spectacles and smiled softly:
"Sir! Other students study for their personal livelihood.
I study for the liberation of fifty million human beings!
In my country, my people are crushed under ignorance and caste bondage. The only weapon that can cut through centuries of servitude is the razor-sharp sword of knowledge!
If I sleep, millions of my brethren will remain in slumber for centuries. Every page I devour is a key to unlock the shackles of my people!"

Towering philosophers like John Dewey and Edwin Seligman marveled at his genius.

Proceeding to London, Ambedkar enrolled simultaneously at the London School of Economics and Gray's Inn, securing two doctorates in economics and qualifying as a barrister-at-law.

That boy who had been denied water at school rose through the power of the book to become the supreme architect of the world's largest democracy.
moral: Knowledge acquired through relentless sacrifice is the ultimate equalizer against social tyranny.
witty_quote: Knowledge is the supreme weapon of liberation; tyrants can chain a man's body, but they can never shackle an intellect enriched by books!
